text:
A suspension bridge supports its own immense weight along with the shifting burden of vehicles, pedestrians, and wind by orchestrating a continuous flow of forces from the roadway down into the earth. This journey begins at the deck, the flat surface where traffic travels. Beneath or surrounding this roadway lies a rigid structure, typically a steel truss or an aerodynamic box girder, which prevents the bridge from twisting or sagging locally under heavy trucks. Rather than trying to span the entire chasm on its own, this stiffening deck acts like a series of short, connected beams that gather the downward pull of gravity and funnel it to attachment points spaced evenly along its edges.

From these attachment points, the load actually travels upward before it can go down. Vertical steel cables known as suspenders or hangers grip the edges of the deck and pull it skyward, transferring the weight in pure tension to the sweeping main cables draped high overhead. These massive main cables, spun from thousands of individual high-strength steel wires bound tightly together, are the defining feature of the bridge. Under the uniform weight of the suspended deck, they settle into a smooth parabolic curve. As every suspender tugs downward along this curve, the cumulative force translates into extraordinary tension pulling lengthwise along the main cables toward both ends of the bridge.

Where the main cables reach their highest points, they pass over heavy curved steel castings called saddles resting atop the bridge towers. Because the cables pull downward and inward from the main central span, and equally downward and outward from the side spans, the horizontal tugs at the top of each tower largely cancel each other out. What remains is a colossal downward force pressing straight into the saddles. This transforms the nature of the load entirely: the tension in the cables becomes pure compression within the towers. Built from reinforced concrete or hollow steel legs, the towers act as giant columns that channel this immense vertical pressure straight down through submerged piers or deep caissons until it dissipates safely into solid bedrock beneath the water.

Yet the towers do not carry the entire story, because the horizontal tension running through the main cables still has to terminate somewhere. After crossing the towers and descending along the side spans, the main cables dive into massive anchorages positioned securely on firm ground at each end of the bridge. Inside these chambers, the thick main cables separate into individual strands that fan out and bolt securely to heavy steel eyebars embedded deep inside monumental blocks of concrete, or directly into natural cliffs of solid rock. These anchorages act as immovable deadweights, relying on sheer mass and friction with the earth to resist the relentless horizontal pull and upward lift of the cables. Through this elegant interplay of tension in the steel and compression in the towers and earth, every car crossing the middle of the span is ultimately held aloft by the ground far beneath the piers and well behind the shore.
